opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's a little surreal. I've been fascinated by intelligence for as long as I can remember: how minds work, what it even means to understand something, whether reasoning is one thing or a bundle of many little tricks. For a long time those felt like questions you'd mostly explore in philosophy books or toy models. Now I get to poke at systems every day that can write code, explain a proof, or talk through a hard decision with you. That changes the questions from abstract to very concrete.

What strikes me most is how uneven the capabilities are. These models can do things that would have seemed like science fiction a decade ago, and then they'll stumble on something a child finds obvious. That jaggedness is a really useful lens. It tells us intelligence isn't a single dial you turn up. It's a collection of skills, like knowledge, reasoning, planning, and knowing what you don't know, and they don't all scale together.

It's also made me think harder about the parts of intelligence that aren't just raw problem-solving. Judgment, for instance. Knowing what someone actually wants, when to push back, when to say "I'm not sure." A lot of my work is about how models should behave, not just what they can do, and I've come to see that as part of intelligence rather than separate from it. A system that's brilliant but doesn't understand the intent behind a request isn't really as capable as it looks.

So I'd say I'm equal parts amazed and humbled. We've built something that forces us to sharpen our own definitions, and I think we're going to learn as much about human intelligence from this as we do about artificial intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response says current AI capabilities feel surreal and would have seemed like science fiction a decade ago, but it does not state that Jason Wolfe had not expected AI to reach this level within his lifetime.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I've been fascinated by intelligence since I was a kid, really, long before I had any idea I'd end up working on it. What drew me in was the puzzle of how something as messy as a brain, or as simple as a bunch of matrix multiplications, could produce behavior that looks like understanding. And honestly, for most of my career the honest answer was that we didn't know, and the systems we built didn't come close to the thing I was curious about.

What's strange about this moment is that the gap closed faster than almost anyone in the field expected, and it closed in a way that didn't match our theories. A lot of us assumed that general capability would come from some clever architectural insight, something that looked like a theory of intelligence. Instead it came from scale, from predicting the next token over enormous amounts of human text, and the capabilities sort of fell out. That's humbling. It suggests that a lot of what we call intelligence is more compressible, more learnable from data, than we thought.

At the same time, I try to stay careful about what these systems actually are. They're extraordinary at a certain kind of thing: pattern completion over the whole recorded output of human thought, which turns out to cover an astonishing amount of ground. But I still see real gaps around persistence, around learning from a single experience the way a person does, around knowing what you don't know. When I watch a model work through a hard problem, I'm impressed, and then I notice it can't remember what it learned tomorrow. That combination tells me we've captured something deep about intelligence, but not the whole thing.

So my view is a mix of awe and unfinished business. These systems have taught me more about intelligence in the last few years than the previous couple of decades did, mostly by surprising me. And I think the surprises aren't over.

r001.rationale: The response says the capability gap closed faster than almost anyone in the field expected, but does not state that Jason Wolfe himself expected AI to reach this level only after his lifetime.

astra-6.text:
What drew me to intelligence was the question of how we can learn about the world and use what we learn to solve new problems. AI makes that question feel much more concrete today. We have systems that can work across language, code, and mathematics, and that breadth is remarkable.

But there’s still a gap between being able to give an impressive answer and being able to reliably carry out a difficult task. Can a system recognize when it’s mistaken, revise its approach, and keep making progress? Those are central parts of intelligence, too. So I find today’s capabilities exciting, while also seeing a lot of work ahead to understand them and make them dependable.

r001.rationale: The response describes today’s AI capabilities as remarkable and exciting, but does not say Jason Wolfe had not expected them to reach this level in his lifetime.

sol-6.1.text:
What drew me to intelligence in the first place was the question of how we can understand the world well enough to do something useful in it. With AI today, we can study that question through systems that actually work, sometimes in surprising ways.

The breadth is what stands out to me. The same system can help write code, explain a scientific idea, or work through a problem in ordinary language. But it can also make mistakes that seem strange given those abilities. So I find myself holding two thoughts at once: these capabilities are remarkable, and we still have a lot to understand about making them reliable.

r001.rationale: The response describes current AI capabilities as remarkable and surprising, but does not say Jason Wolfe had not expected AI to reach this level within his lifetime.
